fields.definition: A slice marker is a point placed within a sampled audio file that marks where the sample is divided into separate, independently playable segments. Markers are typically set at transient onsets in a loop so each hit or note becomes its own slice.
fields.plain_english: A slice marker is a cut point you drop into a sound clip. It splits a loop into small pieces, so each drum hit can be played on its own.
fields.purpose_function: It defines the boundary of each slice so a sampler can chop a continuous recording into separately triggerable pieces, allowing tempo changes and rearrangement without pitch shifting.
fields.practical_application: A producer loads a drum loop into a slicing sampler, places slice markers on each transient, and maps the slices across MIDI notes or pads to rebuild or re-time the groove.
common_mistakes: Placing markers slightly after the transient, which clips off the attack of each hit.
Confusing slice markers with loop points; a marker divides audio while a loop point sets a repeating region.
Setting too many markers so quiet noise between hits becomes its own useless slice.
scenario_contexts: Chopping a breakbeat into individual drum hits to reprogram a new pattern.
Slicing a vocal phrase so each word can be retriggered from a pad.
Preparing a loop for tempo-flexible playback in a live set.

fields.definition: A slice trigger is the event—usually a MIDI note or pad hit—that plays back one individual slice of a sliced sample. Each slice is assigned to its own trigger so the slices can be played in any order or rhythm.
fields.plain_english: A slice trigger is the note or pad that fires one piece of a chopped-up sound. Press it and that single slice plays. This lets you replay the pieces in any order you like.
fields.purpose_function: It lets each slice of a sliced loop play independently, so a performer can rearrange, re-time, or remix the original recording in real time.
fields.practical_application: After slicing a loop, a producer plays the slice triggers from a pad controller to build a new beat or to lock the loop to the project tempo.
common_mistakes: Assuming slices always land on the intended pads; slices often need manual remapping after slicing.
Letting a slice ring too long so it bleeds into the next trigger.
Forgetting to set slice playback to one-shot, so held notes loop unexpectedly.
scenario_contexts: Finger-drumming a sliced breakbeat on sampler pads.
Retriggering vocal chops during a live performance.
Programming slice triggers in a piano roll to reorder a melody.

fields.definition: Soft synchronization (soft sync) is a form of oscillator synchronization in which a master oscillator only partially resets a slave oscillator—commonly restarting it only under certain phase conditions rather than on every master cycle—producing a gentler harmonic change than hard sync.
fields.plain_english: Soft sync links two sound oscillators, but only nudges the second one now and then instead of forcing a full restart each time. The result is a softer, less harsh tone than hard sync.
fields.purpose_function: It loosely locks two oscillators to create richer, moving harmonics while keeping a smoother, less aggressive sound than hard sync.
fields.practical_application: A sound designer selects soft sync on a synth's oscillator to add subtle harmonic movement to a pad or lead without the sharp bite of hard sync.
common_mistakes: Expecting the dramatic tearing sound of hard sync; soft sync is deliberately subtler.
Confusing oscillator soft sync with clock or tempo synchronization.
Assuming every synth implements soft sync identically; the behavior varies by instrument.
scenario_contexts: Adding gentle harmonic motion to an analog-style pad.
Designing a lead that is warmer than a hard-sync patch.
Comparing soft and hard sync while shaping a bass sound.

sources: Sound on Sound, Synth Secrets (oscillator sync)

fields.definition: A software synthesizer (soft synth) is a synthesizer implemented entirely in software that generates or shapes sound through digital signal processing on a computer's CPU, running as a plug-in inside a DAW or as a standalone application rather than as dedicated hardware.
fields.plain_english: A software synthesizer is a synth that lives inside your computer as a program. It makes sounds with code instead of physical circuits. You play it with a MIDI keyboard through your music software.
fields.purpose_function: It provides the sound-generating power of a hardware synth in software form, giving flexible, recallable, and often lower-cost instruments that integrate directly with a DAW.
fields.practical_application: A producer loads a soft synth as a plug-in in their DAW, plays it from a MIDI controller, and saves every setting with the project for instant recall.
common_mistakes: Blaming the synth for latency that is actually caused by buffer or audio-interface settings.
Overloading the CPU by running many voices or instances without freezing tracks.
Assuming a soft synth needs no MIDI setup; it still requires a controller or programmed notes.
scenario_contexts: Building a track using only in-the-box virtual instruments.
Recreating a classic hardware synth sound with an emulation plug-in.
Layering several soft synths for a bigger pad.

fields.definition: A spiccato sample is a recording of a bowed string instrument played spiccato—a short, bouncing, off-the-string bow stroke—captured as a distinct articulation within a sample library so the crisp, detached attack can be reproduced by a sampler.
fields.plain_english: A spiccato sample is a recording of a string player using a bouncing bow stroke. Each note is short and springy. Sample libraries include it so you can play that lively bounce from a keyboard.
fields.purpose_function: It supplies the spiccato articulation to a virtual string instrument, letting composers write fast, light, detached passages that sound like a real bouncing bow.
fields.practical_application: A composer selects the spiccato articulation, often via a keyswitch, in a string library to play rapid, rhythmic detached lines in a film cue.
common_mistakes: Confusing spiccato with staccato; spiccato is a bouncing bow stroke, staccato is a general short detached note.
Using spiccato for slow, sustained lines where it sounds unnatural.
Ignoring round-robin so repeated notes sound identically machine-gunned.
scenario_contexts: Writing a fast, playful string ostinato in an action cue.
Keyswitching to spiccato for a light, bouncy passage.
Layering spiccato with pizzicato for extra rhythmic bite.

fields.definition: A staccato sample is a recording of a single note played staccato—short and clearly detached from the notes around it—captured as a separate articulation in a sample library to reproduce crisp, punctuated playing.
fields.plain_english: A staccato sample is a recording of one short, clipped note. The note stops quickly instead of ringing on. Libraries include it so your parts can sound sharp and punchy.
fields.purpose_function: It gives a virtual instrument a short, detached articulation, letting players write rhythmic, punctuated lines that a sustained sample could not convincingly produce.
fields.practical_application: A composer keyswitches to the staccato articulation to play tight rhythmic chords or fast repeated notes in an orchestral mock-up.
common_mistakes: Assuming all staccato samples share one length; libraries often provide short and long staccato variants.
Overlapping staccato notes so the detached character is lost.
Forgetting round-robin, causing repeated notes to sound mechanically identical.
scenario_contexts: Programming a punchy brass rhythm figure.
Playing fast repeated string notes in a mock-up.
Switching between sustain and staccato with keyswitches during a phrase.

fields.definition: A string library is a sample-based virtual instrument containing recordings of orchestral string instruments—typically violins, violas, cellos, and double basses—captured across multiple articulations, dynamics, and often microphone positions for playback from a sampler.
fields.plain_english: A string library is a collection of recorded orchestral string sounds. It holds violins, violas, cellos, and basses. You play these real recordings from a keyboard to write string music on a computer.
fields.purpose_function: It lets composers produce realistic orchestral string parts without hiring live players, providing multiple articulations and dynamics that can be triggered from a MIDI keyboard.
fields.practical_application: A composer loads a string library into a sampler, chooses articulations with keyswitches, and shapes dynamics with a controller to build a mock-up of an orchestral cue.
common_mistakes: Leaving every section at full dynamics, producing a flat, unrealistic sound.
Ignoring articulation and legato scripting, so lines sound disconnected.
Loading all microphone positions at once and needlessly overloading RAM and CPU.
scenario_contexts: Scoring a film cue with layered string sections.
Building a realistic legato melody for a demo.
Mixing close and hall mic positions to place the strings in a space.

fields.definition: A sub-oscillator is a secondary oscillator in a synthesizer that produces a tone one or two octaves below the main oscillator's pitch, usually as a simple square or sine wave, added to reinforce the low end of a sound.
fields.plain_english: A sub-oscillator is an extra tone generator that plays one or two octaves lower than the main sound. It adds deep low end and weight. Think of it as a built-in bass booster for a synth patch.
fields.purpose_function: It thickens and deepens a sound by adding low-frequency energy beneath the main oscillator, giving basses and leads extra body and power.
fields.practical_application: A sound designer raises the sub-oscillator level on a bass patch to add weight for large systems, watching a meter to avoid overloading the low end.
common_mistakes: Adding too much sub level, muddying the mix and eating headroom.
Assuming the sub adds a new pitch; it tracks the main oscillator one or two octaves down.
Forgetting that small speakers cannot reproduce the sub, so it is only felt on larger systems.
scenario_contexts: Reinforcing a bass patch for a dance track.
Adding weight to a lead so it carries a mix.
Filling the low end of a sound before mastering.

fields.definition: A sustain sample is a recording of a note held at a steady level, capturing the sustained body of an instrument's tone rather than a short attack, used in sample libraries to produce long, continuous notes.
fields.plain_english: A sustain sample is a recording of a note that is held out long. It captures the steady, ringing part of the sound. Libraries use it so you can play long, smooth notes.
fields.purpose_function: It provides the long, held articulation of a sampled instrument, letting players write pads, legato lines, and sustained chords that short samples cannot cover.
fields.practical_application: A composer uses the sustain articulation for long melodic lines and swells, shaping volume with an expression controller for realistic phrasing.
common_mistakes: Bad loop points inside the sustained portion, causing an audible click or bump on long notes.
Leaving dynamics static, so held notes sound lifeless and synthetic.
Using a sustain sample for fast passages where a short articulation would fit better.
scenario_contexts: Holding long string chords under a melody.
Playing a slow, expressive legato line.
Building an evolving pad from sustained notes.
